steps.caption: The **H gene** adds L-fucose to a precursor chain, making H antigen; without a working H gene (Bombay, hh) no H, A or B antigen is made. The A gene's transferase then adds N-acetyl-D-galactosamine (A antigen) and the B gene's adds D-galactose (B antigen). The O gene makes no working enzyme, so group O cells keep the most H.
A, B and O are alleles at one locus; A and B are codominant and O is silent. An **AO × BO** couple can have children of all four groups, each with a 1 in 4 chance: AB, A (AO), B (BO) and O (OO).
**Forward typing** tests the patient's red cells with anti-A and anti-B reagents. Agglutination (+) shows which antigens are on the cells.

**Reverse typing** tests the patient's plasma with A1 and B reagent cells. Plasma has antibodies to the A or B antigen the cells lack (**Landsteiner's rule**): group A has anti-B, group B has anti-A, group O has both, group AB has neither.
**To remember:** forward (cells) and reverse (plasma) results must agree. If they don't, it's an **ABO discrepancy**, and it must be resolved before the group is reported.

visuals.alt: Three panels. 1: the H gene adds L-fucose to a precursor chain to make H antigen; the A gene adds N-acetyl-D-galactosamine (A antigen), the B gene adds D-galactose (B antigen), and the O gene adds nothing, so group O keeps the most H. 2: a Punnett square for AO × BO parents giving AB, AO (group A), BO (group B) and OO (group O), one in four each. 3: a typing table. Forward typing (cells with anti-A, anti-B): A is + and 0; B is 0 and +; AB is + and +; O is 0 and 0. Reverse typing (plasma with A1 cells, B cells): A is 0 and +; B is + and 0; AB is 0 and 0; O is + and +.

steps.caption: **IgG** is a monomer: two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains (kappa or lambda), held together by disulfide (S–S) bonds.

Each arm is a **Fab**; its tip binds antigen, so IgG has 2 binding sites. The stem is the **Fc**, which binds Fc receptors and complement. Papain cuts at the **hinge** into 2 Fab + 1 Fc; pepsin cuts below it, giving one F(ab')2.
IgG is the **only class that crosses the placenta** (its Fc is carried across actively). That is why maternal IgG antibodies cause HDFN.
**IgM** is a pentamer: five monomers joined by disulfide bonds and one **J chain**. That gives 10 antigen-binding sites. IgM is the first antibody made in a primary response.

With so many binding sites, IgM is the best at **agglutination** and at activating complement: one IgM bound to a cell can start the classical pathway, while IgG needs two molecules side by side. IgM is too big to cross the placenta.
**To remember:** IgG = monomer, 2 sites, crosses the placenta. IgM = pentamer with a J chain, 10 sites, best agglutinator and complement activator, does not cross.

visuals.alt: Top: an IgG monomer drawn as a Y. Two solid heavy chains form the stem and continue into each arm; a hatched light chain lies along the outer side of each arm. Disulfide bonds join the heavy chains at the hinge and each light chain to its heavy chain. Each arm is a Fab with an antigen-binding site at its tip (2 sites); the stem is the Fc, which binds Fc receptors and complement C1q. A note says only IgG crosses the placenta. Bottom: an IgM pentamer, five Y-shaped monomers radiating from a disulfide-linked centre with one J chain, giving 10 antigen-binding sites. A note says IgM is best at agglutination and complement activation and is too big to cross the placenta.

steps.caption: The **direct antiglobulin test (DAT)** asks whether the patient's red cells are already coated with antibody or complement in the body (in vivo). The cells are washed and AHG is added straight away, with no incubation.

Use the DAT when cells may be coated in vivo: **HDFN** (the baby's cells coated by maternal IgG), hemolytic **transfusion reactions** (donor cells coated by the recipient's antibody), and **autoimmune or drug-induced** hemolytic anemia.

The **indirect antiglobulin test (IAT)** asks whether the patient's serum has antibody to red cell antigens. Serum and reagent cells are incubated at 37 °C so antibody can coat the cells in vitro; then they are washed and AHG is added.

Washing removes unbound globulin, which would neutralize the AHG and cause a false negative. Every negative tube test read with an anti-IgG–containing AHG gets **IgG-coated check cells**: they must agglutinate, proving AHG was added and not neutralized by leftover globulin.

Use the IAT to find antibodies before transfusion: the **antibody screen**, antibody identification and the **AHG crossmatch**. The same method detects antigens with IgG reagents, such as the **weak D** test.

**To remember:** DAT = coated in vivo, no incubation (HDFN, transfusion reaction, AIHA). IAT = coated in vitro after 37 °C incubation (screen, crossmatch). Both are washed, get AHG, and negatives are checked with check cells.

visuals.alt: Two flow columns. DAT (direct): patient's red cells from an EDTA sample, no incubation, wash 3 to 4 times, add AHG and centrifuge, read; clumping means the cells were coated in the body. IAT (indirect): patient's serum plus reagent red cells, incubate at 37 °C so antibody coats the cells, wash, add AHG and centrifuge, read; clumping means antibody in the serum. If either is negative, IgG-coated check cells are added and must agglutinate or the test is invalid. DAT uses: HDFN, transfusion reactions, autoimmune and drug-induced hemolytic anemia. IAT uses: antibody screen and identification, AHG crossmatch, weak D and antigen typing.

steps.caption: **Classical pathway:** C1q binds antibody (IgM, or IgG) that is bound to antigen. C1r activates C1s, which splits C4 and C2 to build the C3 convertase **C4b2a** (newer texts, which rename the large C2 fragment C2b, write C4b2b).
**Lectin pathway:** mannose-binding lectin (MBL) binds carbohydrates on microbes, with no antibody needed. Its MASPs split C4 and C2 just as C1s does, making the same **C4b2a**.
**Alternative pathway:** C3 hydrolyzes slowly on its own (tickover). Factor B binds, factor D cleaves it, and the C3 convertase **C3bBb** forms; **properdin** stabilizes it.
All three pathways meet at **C3**. Each C3 convertase splits C3 into **C3a**, an anaphylatoxin, and **C3b**, an opsonin that coats cells for phagocytosis.

C3b joins the C3 convertase to make a **C5 convertase**, which splits C5. **C5a** is the most potent anaphylatoxin and attracts neutrophils; C5b binds C6, C7, C8 and C9 to form the **membrane attack complex**, a pore that lyses the cell.
**To remember:** three starts (antibody, MBL, spontaneous C3), one common end. C3b opsonizes, C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins, and C5b-9 lyses.

visuals.alt: Three columns start the complement cascade. Classical: C1q binds antibody bound to antigen; C1r activates C1s, which splits C4 and C2. Lectin: MBL binds mannose on microbes; MASPs split C4 and C2. Both make the C3 convertase C4b2a (written C4b2b in newer nomenclature). Alternative: C3 hydrolyzes on its own; factors B and D act and properdin stabilizes the C3 convertase C3bBb. All C3 convertases split C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin). C3b joins to form the C5 convertase (C4b2a3b or C3bBb3b), which splits C5 into C5a (anaphylatoxin, chemotaxis) and C5b. C5b with C6, C7, C8 and many C9 forms the membrane attack complex C5b-9, a pore that lyses the cell.

steps.caption: In a **sandwich ELISA**, the well is coated with a **capture antibody** specific for the antigen to be measured.
The patient sample is added. Antigen, if present, is caught by the capture antibody; a wash then removes everything unbound.
An **enzyme-labeled detection antibody** (E) binds another site on the antigen, completing the sandwich. A second wash removes unbound labeled antibody, so enzyme stays only where antigen was caught.
Substrate is added and the enzyme turns it into a colored product. The color is **directly proportional** to the amount of antigen in the sample.

An **indirect ELISA** measures antibody instead (for example, HIV antibody screening). The well is coated with antigen, patient antibody binds it, and an **enzyme-labeled anti-human IgG** detects the bound patient antibody.

**To remember:** sandwich = capture antibody, antigen, enzyme-labeled antibody, so it measures **antigen**. Indirect = antigen, patient antibody, enzyme-labeled anti-IgG, so it measures **antibody**. Wash between every layer.

visuals.alt: Top row, sandwich ELISA in four panels: 1, capture antibodies coat the well; 2, sample antigen (diamonds) binds them, then a wash; 3, enzyme-labeled detection antibodies (marked E) bind the antigen, then a wash; 4, substrate is added and colored product forms around each enzyme. A small graph shows color rising in direct proportion to the amount of antigen. Bottom row, indirect ELISA: 1, antigen coats the well; 2, patient serum antibody binds, then a wash; 3, enzyme-labeled anti-human IgG binds the patient antibody, then a wash; 4, substrate gives color.

visuals.subject: BB
visuals.title: Hepatitis B serologic markers

steps.caption: In acute hepatitis B, **HBsAg** is the first serologic marker to appear, before symptoms. **HBeAg** follows; it marks active viral replication and high infectivity.
**Anti-HBc** appears around the time symptoms start. The IgM form marks recent infection and fades over months; total anti-HBc stays for life after any infection.
As HBeAg disappears, **anti-HBe** appears. This seroconversion means replication and infectivity are falling.

The **core window**: HBsAg has gone but anti-HBs is not yet detectable, so **anti-HBc (IgM)** is the only marker of recent infection; anti-HBe may also be present. Do not confuse it with the donor-screening window period, the early time before HBsAg is detectable.
**Anti-HBs** appears after HBsAg is gone and persists: it marks recovery and immunity.
**To remember:** after recovery, anti-HBc and anti-HBs are both positive. A **vaccinated** person has anti-HBs only, because the vaccine contains only HBsAg.

visuals.alt: Schematic curves over time after exposure, no numbers. Viral antigens: HBsAg appears first, rises and falls; HBeAg appears just after it and disappears sooner. Antibodies: total anti-HBc rises around symptom onset and stays for life; IgM anti-HBc rises at the same time, then fades over months; anti-HBe appears as HBeAg disappears and persists at a lower level; anti-HBs appears last, after HBsAg is gone, and persists. A dashed band marks the core window between the loss of HBsAg and the appearance of anti-HBs, when IgM anti-HBc is the marker of recent infection. A table compares recovered infection (HBsAg negative, total anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs positive) with vaccination (anti-HBs positive only).

steps.caption: Rh HDFN needs a **D-negative mother** carrying a **D-positive fetus**, who inherited D from the father. The placenta keeps the two circulations apart, so a first pregnancy is usually unaffected.

At **delivery** (or abortion, amniocentesis or trauma), a **fetomaternal hemorrhage** (FMH) lets fetal D+ cells into her blood. She makes **IgM anti-D** first, which cannot cross the placenta, then **IgG** and memory B cells.

In the **next D-positive pregnancy**, memory cells quickly make **IgG anti-D**, which crosses the placenta and coats the fetal D+ cells. The coated cells are destroyed in the fetal spleen (extravascular hemolysis).

The baby becomes **anemic**, with erythroblasts in the blood (erythroblastosis fetalis) and hydrops if severe. Before birth the mother's liver clears the bilirubin, so it rises fast **after birth**; the newborn's **DAT is positive**.

**Prevention:** a D-negative, unimmunized mother gets **RhIG** at about **28 weeks** and again within **72 hours** of delivering a D-positive (including weak D) baby; it clears fetal D+ cells before she can respond. The **rosette test** screens for a large bleed, and if positive a **Kleihauer–Betke** stain sets the dose: one 300 µg vial per 30 mL of fetal whole blood.

**ABO HDFN** is usually mild. It occurs mostly in **group O** mothers, whose IgG anti-A,B can affect even the **first** baby; A and B antigens are weak on fetal cells, so the **DAT is weak** or negative and the smear shows **spherocytes**. RhIG does not prevent it.

visuals.alt: Rh HDFN in panels. First pregnancy: a D-negative mother and a D-positive fetus separated by the placenta. At delivery, a fetomaternal hemorrhage carries fetal D-positive cells into the mother. She is sensitized: a B cell makes IgM anti-D first, then IgG and memory cells. In the next D-positive pregnancy, her IgG anti-D crosses the placenta and coats the fetal cells, which are destroyed; the baby is anemic with erythroblasts and possibly hydrops, bilirubin rises after birth, and the newborn DAT is positive. Prevention: RhIG at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery of a D-positive baby, given to D-negative unimmunized mothers; it coats the fetal cells in her blood. The dose is set by a rosette test, then a Kleihauer-Betke stain if positive: percent fetal cells times 50 gives mL of fetal whole blood, divided by 30 per 300 microgram vial, rounded, plus one vial. A table compares Rh and ABO HDFN: mother D-negative versus group O; IgG anti-D made after exposure versus IgG anti-A,B already present; first baby rarely versus can be affected; can be severe versus usually mild; DAT strongly positive versus weak or negative; nucleated red cells versus spherocytes; prevented by RhIG versus not preventable.

steps.caption: In **Fisher-Race** (CDE) terms, each chromosome carries one **haplotype**: D or no D, C or c, and E or e, inherited together. The small d only means D is absent; there is no d antigen and no anti-d.

**Wiener** wrote each haplotype as one symbol. Capital **R** means D is present and small **r** means it is absent; 1 or ' adds C, 2 or '' adds E, z or y adds both, and 0 or no mark means c and e. So R1 = DCe, r' = dCe and ry = dCE.

Each antigen has a name in every system: D = **Rh₀** = Rh1, C = rh' = Rh2, E = rh'' = Rh3, c = hr' = Rh4, e = hr'' = Rh5. **Rosenfield** used numbers to record reactions (e.g. Rh:1,2,−3,4,5), and the **ISBT** numbers the Rh system 004, so D is RH1 (004001).

**R1 (DCe)** is the most common haplotype in White and Asian populations, **r (dce)** is next in White populations, and **R0 (Dce)** is the most common in Black populations; Rz, r', r'' and ry are rare. About 15% of White people are D-negative (rr), compared with under 1% of most Asian populations.

**Reading a genotype:** R1r = DCe/dce, so the cells type D+ C+ c+ e+ and E−. The same reactions could come from R1R0 or R0r', but in a White donor R1r is the **most probable** genotype because R1 and r are common.

visuals.alt: A table of the eight Rh haplotypes in Fisher-Race and Wiener notation: Dce = R0, DCe = R1, DcE = R2, DCE = Rz (all D-positive); dce = r, dCe = r', dcE = r'', dCE = ry (all D-negative). The Wiener code: R means D present, r means no D; 1 or prime means C, 2 or double prime means E, z or y means C and E, 0 or no mark means c and e. Frequency: R0 most common in Black populations, R1 most common in White and Asian populations, r second in White populations, R2 common, Rz, r', r'' and ry rare. A second table of antigen names: D = Rh0 (Wiener) = Rh1 (Rosenfield) = RH1 (ISBT system 004); C = rh' = Rh2 = RH2; E = rh'' = Rh3 = RH3; c = hr' = Rh4 = RH4; e = hr'' = Rh5 = RH5. A worked example: R1r = DCe/dce gives D+ C+ c+ e+ E− cells; R1R0 and R0r' give the same reactions, but R1r is the most probable.
